sections.h2: Your regulars run on a three-week clock and nobody's watching it.
paras: A guy who comes in every three weeks sits in your chair about seventeen times a year. Stretch him to five weeks and the same head of hair is worth ten visits. That's arithmetic, not marketing, and it's most of the difference between a strong year and a flat one.

Regulars rarely quit outright. They drift. Something comes up in week four, then it's week seven, then it feels awkward to walk back in. A short message in the right week — not a newsletter, a text that reads like it came from the shop — pulls most of them back onto the clock before the drift hardens into a habit.

sections.h2: Saturday takes care of itself. Tuesday at two is the problem.
paras: Weekends fill whether or not you have a website. What you're leaving on the table sits between eleven and four on a weekday, and the only way to move it is to let someone see the open slot at the moment they think about it: on a break, in a line, waiting on a sandwich.

Online booking that shows real openings, barber by barber, does that quietly. Clients follow the person who cuts their hair rather than the sign over the door, so the booking page names them and holds the chair on the calendar you already keep.
bullets: Booking synced to your Google Calendar, so a slot taken online is gone from the phone too.
Hours that tell the truth — closed Monday, open Sunday morning, shutting early on a holiday weekend.
Walk-ins still walk in. The book shows what's open, it doesn't lock the door.
Your price list on the page — fade, beard, kids, seniors, the full works.

sections.h2: A first-timer decides on his phone, twenty feet from your window.
paras: He isn't reading an About page. He wants four things in roughly the time a light takes to change — are you open now, can you take him today, what does a fade cost, and does the work look like what's in his head. The rest of the page is decoration.

So the first screen answers those four, and your Google Business Profile carries photographs of cuts that actually came out of your shop instead of catalogue models. Then the whole thing loads before he loses interest and taps the next result.

Growth — $500 a month, with $500 once at the start: everything above, and then the CRM, automated review requests, the reminder and follow-up messages, card payments, expenses kept in one place, monthly reports and a clean handoff to QuickBooks.

Ours flags the regular who's two weeks past his usual, sends the message that gets him booked, and asks for the Google review the evening after a good cut. It holds the invoices and what you spent as well, so February makes sense on paper instead of in your gut.

paras: The week the snow finally gives up, every homeowner in the village looks at the lawn on the same morning and starts calling around. Whoever replies that day takes the contract and holds it for the next eight months. Whoever calls back Thursday evening is bidding against somebody who has already cut it once.

So March is a bad month to be running quotes out of a notebook. Requests have to reach your phone the second they're sent — with the address on them — so answering takes thirty seconds between properties instead of an hour after dinner.

sections.h2: Four lawns on one block beat eight scattered across town.
paras: Drive time is the one real cost you can never bill for. A tight route inside one subdivision pays; the same eight accounts spread over four towns pays somebody else. So the site is written around the streets you already run, and the quote form asks for an address before it asks for anything else.
Once you can see where a new request sits against Tuesday's route, you can price it honestly — or price it high on purpose because it's out of the way, and both of you know which one is happening.

sections.h2: Quoting from the truck and invoicing at nine at night is a tax on being busy.
paras: Plenty of crews measure a lawn from a satellite view, send a number, and then lose an evening a week turning a clipboard into invoices. The estimate should leave from the phone while you're still in the driveway and get accepted with a tap.
Recurring cuts go on autopay so nobody's chasing a check in July. One-off work gets invoiced the day it's finished, while the customer can still see how the yard looked when you pulled away.
bullets: Quote requests arriving by property address, straight to your phone — not an inbox you open at ten.
Card on file for weekly and biweekly accounts — charged automatically once the cut is done.
Materials, fuel and dump fees logged against the job, so you know which contracts are genuinely earning.
Every property, price and schedule on one list your crew can pull up in the cab.

sections.h2: Rain rewrites the week, and thirty people want to know if you're coming.
paras: Two wet days in a row and Tuesday's route lands on Thursday, which shoves Thursday into Saturday. The phone starts going while you're still working out the new order. One message to the affected properties settles all of it before anybody has to ask twice.
If the calls keep coming anyway, the answering bolt-on takes them at $100 a month, with every detail captured and waiting in the CRM by the time the trailer is unhitched.

sections.h2: The season doesn't actually end in October.
paras: Leaf cleanup, gutters, the last cut, snow, then spring cleanups and mulch. The customers for every one of those are already on your list — and the winter money is largely a matter of asking the people who trusted you in June.

Automated messages do that asking in the right week of the year — and the ones who say yes book without a phone call at all. That's the whole distance between a mowing route and a year-round business.

sections.h2: What the whole thing costs.
paras: A twelve-month partnership, billed monthly on the same date, with both numbers on the table now.
bullets: Foundation is $250 each month with a one-time $250: website on your domain, Google Business Profile built out, online booking that lands on your calendar, a work email on your own domain, SEO for the towns you cut in, plus two updates a month.

Growth is $500 each month with a one-time $500: everything in Foundation, and then the CRM, review requests that go out on their own, the automatic texts and emails, card payments, expense tracking, monthly reports and a clean feed into your accounting software.
Twelve months paid up front comes to $2,550 or $5,100, which is 15 percent off, with setup billed separately.
Add-ons if you want them: $100 a month for the answering service, $130 a month for review replies, and custom work quoted job by job.

sections.h2: Take the demo out for a run.
paras: Knox Blocks handles quote requests, scheduling and invoices the way a real crew needs them to work. Send yourself an estimate request on it and watch what comes back.
Some crews honestly don't need this. If you're booked solid on word of mouth and you like your evenings the way they are, we'll tell you to keep your $250 — and we'll mean it.

pages.townPara: The streets above Lake Ellyn are the work most crews want. The lake has been there since 1889 and Glenbard West has stood above it at 670 Crescent Blvd since 1923 — so the lots are old, the trees are big, and the neighbors notice a straight stripe from their own driveway. That's ground where a reputation still travels over a fence. It's also where somebody watches your truck work a yard on Wednesday, looks you up on Thursday, and turns up nothing. Word of mouth gets people searching your name; what they find is what decides whether they call.

crmCallout.heading: A route, a price and a schedule for every property.
crmCallout.para: The CRM is a clipboard that never gets left in the truck — every property, what it costs, when it gets cut, and what's been paid. Recurring accounts bill themselves, one-time jobs get invoiced from the driveway, and the customers who only ever hired you for a fall cleanup hear from you again before spring. It carries fuel, materials and dump fees too, so the monthly report tells you what the season is really making.

cta.heading: Try it before the phone starts in March.
cta.para: Open Knox Blocks, send yourself an estimate request, and follow the whole loop through to the invoice. Then call (331) 291-7400 and tell us how many properties you're running.

faqs.q: Can customers get a quote without me driving out there?
faqs.a: For a standard mow, usually. The request arrives with the address, you measure it from an aerial view, and the estimate goes back from your phone. The drive is only worth making for design work and the big cleanups.

faqs.q: Will this handle weekly accounts and one-off jobs at the same time?
faqs.a: Yes. Recurring properties sit on a schedule with a card on file, and one-time work gets quoted, scheduled and invoiced on its own without leaving the same system.

faqs.q: We shut down for the winter. Are we paying for months we don't use?
faqs.a: You are, and it's worth saying that plainly. The twelve-month term doesn't pause. What it buys in the off months is the leaf and snow work, the spring pre-booking, and the site still getting found while nobody is mowing.

pages.formHeading: How many properties are you cutting?
pages.formSub: Give us the number and the towns and we'll tell you what we'd build for it.
